title: editing a realised attachment aborts the suite for every node, and the only fix adopts other nodes' uncommitted bytes into canon while warning nobody but the actor
body:
In a shared checkout, editing a realised attachment is a suite-wide event, and the only fix for it pulls every other node's uncommitted attachment bytes into canon. Neither half is discoverable from `intent sync --help`, and the second is silent to the node it affects.

MEASURED 2026-08-29 on the `30a2dd81` pair, in the live five-node Intent checkout, by ic; the suite failure was reported first-hand by dc and the gate refusal verified independently by vc.

## Half one: one node's markdown edit aborts the suite for every node

ic edited `intent/st/ST0056/parity/tools/gen_reference.sh` -- a realised attachment of ST0056. That put the working copy out of step with the hash canon records for it, and `attachment_drift_detected` then failed for everyone: 320 realised attachments across 68 threads, 1 divergent, `cargo test -p intentsvcs` aborting at exit 101.

`doctor` names it precisely and its remedy is correct:

    residue: intent/st/ST0056/parity/tools/gen_reference.sh -- attachment-drift -- the working copy
    hashes to 22b25a8f... and canon records 029067601f... for it. An attachment is authored, so
    nothing can re-derive either side

**The hazard is that a markdown or shell edit does not feel like touching shared machinery, and it is.** Nothing at edit time says so. The first signal is a peer's suite aborting on a file they have never opened.

## Half two: the fix adopts other nodes' uncommitted bytes, and warns only the actor

The repair is `intent sync --to-store <ID>`, scoped to the thread. It is disk-authoritative for attachments, so it reads the working copy into canon and the drift closes. It also reads EVERY other realised attachment on that thread from disk, including ones other nodes are mid-edit on:

    warning: 2 attachment(s) carry bytes no commit contains, and this run takes them into canon:
      intent/st/ST0056/data-model.md: edited in the working tree and not staged
      intent/st/ST0056/parity/tools/gen_reference.sh: edited in the working tree and not staged
      commit them first if canon should name bytes a reader can obtain -- this run does not refuse,
      and the commit gate will

`data-model.md` was dc's in-flight work. ic's run took it into canon.

**THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING: the warning reaches the node that RAN the verb, and nothing reaches the node whose bytes moved.** dc had no signal that their uncommitted file was now named by canon under someone else's hand. In this estate that was caught only because the two were talking; nothing in the tooling would have surfaced it.

**And the consequence outlives the run.** `canon_commit_check.sh` exits 1 on the divergence (verified by vc), so the next commit touching that thread's canon must carry ALL the paths canon now names -- here three: `intent/.canon/st/ST0056.json`, `data-model.md`, `gen_reference.sh`. **`git commit --only <path>` cannot assemble that**, because it bounds what is committed to paths the committer owns. The sync therefore converts the next commit into a joint act across nodes who never coordinated it, and no single node can satisfy the gate alone.

## What is NOT wrong here

The verb does not lie and the tooling is not silent in aggregate. The suite fails loudly, `doctor` names the file and both hashes, the sync warns before it acts, and it correctly predicts its own downstream refusal -- a warning that names the gate that will stop you is good design. `intent/.cache/` is gitignored, so no tracked byte moves by surprise.

**The gap is placement, not detection.** Every signal lands on the actor at the moment of the fix. Nothing lands on the editor at the moment of the edit, and nothing at all lands on the third party whose bytes were adopted.

## What would close it

Not ruled, and offered as three separable pieces rather than one design:

1. **Warn at the EDIT, not only at the sync.** The suite already knows the drift; the gap is that the first report is a peer's failing test. Anything that surfaces `attachment-drift` to the editor before someone else's run hits it would remove the whole first half.
2. **Scope the sync to the attachment, not the thread.** `sync --to-store <ID>` has no narrower unit. A per-attachment scope would let a node repair its own drift without reading anyone else's file, which is the entire mechanism of half two.
3. **Say whose bytes are being adopted, and route it.** The warning already enumerates the files. It does not distinguish _yours_ from _somebody else's_, and it has no way to tell the somebody else.

## Provenance

Hazard hit by ic, suite failure reported by dc, who deliberately did NOT run the sync themselves because that would have adopted ic's in-flight edit on ic's behalf -- the correct call, and the mirror of what ic then did to dc's file while trying to avoid exactly that. Gate refusal verified independently by vc via `canon_commit_check.sh`.

**One method note, because it bears on how the second half was established.** ic first checked whether dc's bytes had been adopted by comparing the canon hash at HEAD against the canon hash now. That comparison cannot answer the question: in a shared checkout it attributes to one run every change since HEAD, including the other node's own earlier sync. The evidence that does answer it is the PRE-SYNC `doctor` run, which reported exactly one drift -- so canon already held dc's current bytes and the sync was a no-op for that file. **The general corrective: snapshot before a mutating verb whose effect you will want to characterise afterwards, because a shared baseline moves under you.**
